text:
Celery.
DIFFICULTY
Difficult
5/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn / Winter

Celery needs rich, moist, weed-free soil for crisp, well-flavoured stems. Traditional trench celery needs deep preparation, regular watering and earthing-up to exclude light for winter stems. Self-blanching types are easier: close planting and a dense canopy help blanch them, but they are less hardy and best cut before cold weather. Celery leaf gives repeated pickings of smaller stems. Dry checks cause bitterness, stringiness and bolting; slugs can spoil appearance without affecting flavour.

Quick facts
Sow indoors

Mar–Apr. A May sowing is for leaf celery.

Harvest

Sep – Jan

Germination

12–21 days

Yield (10 ft row)

12 lb

Plant out

Late May–Jun after frost.

Sowing depth

Surface sow or barely cover with fine compost

Row spacing

Trench rows: about 3 ft 3 in.; blocks: 10 in. each way.

Plant spacing

Trench types: 12–18 in. between plants; self-blanching/green: 10 in. each way.

Ready in

From sowing: self-blanching ~25 weeks; trench types ~40 weeks

Recommended varieties
SELF BLANCHING
Victoria F1

Self-blanching celery with crisp, pale stalks. Easier than trench types.

SELF BLANCHING
Golden Self-Blanching

Traditional pale self-blanching celery. Water regularly for tender stalks.

SELF BLANCHING
Green Utah

Green-stemmed celery with a strong flavour. Keep moist for steady growth and tender stalks.

TRENCH
Giant Red

Red-stemmed trench celery with a strong flavour. Needs blanching and winter protection.

Key risks
Bolting

Bolting is a serious problem, especially in dry seasons or where young plants have been checked.

Slugs and snails

Slugs and snails chew celery leaves and stems, especially in damp conditions.

Celery fly (leaf miner)

Larvae mine celery leaves, making pale blotches that turn brown and papery.

Celery leaf spot (blight)

Brown or yellowish-brown spots appear first on the outer leaflets and then spread to all of the foliage.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
42
STALKS & SHOOTS

Rich soil and steady moisture.

Plenty of compost or manure helps on drier ground.

Do not let celery dry out.

Dry spells make stems tough and stringy and encourage bolting.

Mulch and feed where needed.

Keep mulch clear of stem bases; feed hungry summer crops.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, humus-filled soil kept evenly moist. Add compost or well-rotted manure; do not lime routinely.
Prepare traditional trenches as follows: Trench types: 12 in. deep, 18 in. wide; refill with soil and compost to 4 in. below ground.
Sowing & planting
Raise seedlings
Plant a block
Sow indoors 

Scatter seed on damp compost and barely cover it. Keep warm, light and ventilated. Move seedlings into individual pots when large enough to handle.

Plant out 

Harden off without chilling the plants. Set green and self-blanching celery at module depth in a close block. Water well, especially during the first two weeks in dry weather.

Trench celery 

Plant trench varieties in a prepared trench at their wider spacing. The stems can be earthed up as they lengthen.

Looking after the crop
Keep the root zone evenly moist. Dry spells make stems tough and stringy.
Mulch clear of stem bases. Feed organically if growth is weak.
Earth up trench celery as stems lengthen. Tie the tops, draw soil around the stems, keep the heart clear, then untie.
Excluding light makes stems paler, crisper and less bitter. Self-blanching types need close planting and steady moisture, but no trench.
Shield young plants from cold to prevent bolting. Mature trench types are hardier than self-blanching; protect in severe frost. Wear gloves and long sleeves: sap can irritate skin.
Harvesting & storage
Cut self-blanching celery before frost or toughening. Cutting above soil may allow a small second picking in mild weather.
Pick larger outside stems of celery leaf regularly to encourage new growth.
Harvest trench celery in late autumn–early winter.
Lift from a row end, replacing soil around remaining plants. Keep stalks cool and use promptly.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting	A flower stalk replaces usable stems.	Water evenly. Harden off and plant after frost.
Slugs and snails	Holes in leaves and stems; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick on damp evenings and clear dead leaves.
Celery fly (leaf miner)	Blistered leaves	Tolerate light damage; pinch out mined parts or mesh a rotated bed.
Celery leaf spot (blight)	Spotted leaves	Remove affected leaves. Use clean seed and avoid stale, wet conditions.
Final tips

Wear gloves and long sleeves when tending celery; sap can irritate skin.

Check for slugs; keep earth out of the heart.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 115–116 · Growing Techniques 150
43
